subject: odd results and warning message, NaNs produced, for occupancy analysis...

messages.author: 46668c7abb49655f
messages.subject: odd results and warning message, NaNs produced, for occupancy analysis...
parts:
Hello,

I had very recently posted a question pertaining to occupancy analysis of rats in an archipelago in Micronesia, and issues I encountered using “linearComb” during the process.  Now, another data set from that project regarding a species of ground-nesting bird.  I did surveys for this species on the same islands as those I surveyed for rats.  Because of time constraints I could only get one survey visit in over one rather brief field season (I was actually lucky to get these data at all).  I surveyed a total of 48 stations, 19 on islands visited by tourists and the remaining 29 on islands not visited by tourists (the number of stations was based on the area of accessible habitat on each island).  I did playback surveys and got counts of individual birds per station – but I have no distance data so I can’t estimate density of abundance.

 

Although I can calculate relative abundance, these data are still presence / absence.  To assess occupancy in unmarked, I changed my detections to 1 (for birds detected) and 0 (no birds detected) per station.  However, for some reason that I can’t put my finger on, I’m getting results that don’t make sense.  I suspect there is something very simple I’m overlooking (as a result of my relative inexperience with unmarked) in terms of how I’m trying to analyse these data, but I can’t see it.  When using “occu” to analyse for occupancy and probability of detection with the covariate ("Tourist") not included, I come up with this, the same results for each:

Call:
occu(formula = ~1 ~ 1, data = meg_occu)

Occupancy:
 Estimate  SE       z P(>|z|)
     1.87 564 0.00331   0.997

Detection:
 Estimate  SE       z P(>|z|)
     1.87 564 0.00331   0.997

AIC: 57.98417 
> backTransform(fm1, 'state')
Backtransformed linear combination(s) of Occupancy estimate(s)

 Estimate   SE LinComb (Intercept)
    0.866 65.4    1.87           1

Transformation: logistic 
> backTransform(fm1, 'det')
Backtransformed linear combination(s) of Detection estimate(s)

 Estimate   SE LinComb (Intercept)
    0.866 65.4    1.87           1


When I run this for fm2, i.e., including the covariate ("Tourist"), I get this...

Call:
occu(formula = ~Tourist ~ 1, data = meg_occu)

Occupancy:
 Estimate  SE   z P(>|z|)
     2.92 NaN NaN     NaN

Detection:
            Estimate  SE   z P(>|z|)
(Intercept)     3.97 NaN NaN     NaN
Tourist        -3.97 NaN NaN     NaN

AIC: 46.84232 
Warning messages:
1: In sqrt(diag(vcov(obj))) : NaNs produced
2: In sqrt(diag(vcov(obj))) : NaNs produced

So, where am I going wrong here?  Is "occu" the incorrect model-fitting function in this case?  Or, does the issue lie in the fact that I'm analysing for only one visit or replicate instead of multiple???

Thanks - I appreciate your time...
Paul

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] odd results and warning message, NaNs produced, for occupancy analysis...
parts:
Dear Paul,

couple of things.

First, with only a single visit, one cannot separately estimate occupancy and detection probability. This explains the strange result (you see twice the same numbers). You must ignore this. (When you have continuous covariates, and some affect exclusively occupancy and the other(s) exclusively detection, you can separately estimate both components of the model, but such an analysis may not be very robust and care has to be taken).

Second, you have count data and hence much more information about the local populations than just presence/absence. I would convert counts to detection/nondetection data only very exceptionally, since you throw out information. In your case, I would fit a Poisson regression, knowing and acknowledging openly that the modelled quantity is not the expected abundance, but the expectation of the product of abundance and detection at each site. This is what 80-90% of all people in Ecology do, so it is unlikely that you will be slayed. Think hard about possible covariates that could act on detection and that, in your case, will show up on the expectation of abundance and detection: they can feign a relationship with abundance that's not there, make it weaker or stronger or mask it. Discuss this.

For single-visit count data, there is also the possibility to separate detection and abundance with continuous covariates,  but I would not recommend such an analysis, because it is extremely dependent on the parametric assumptions of the model, see http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12507/abstract and also http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12329/abstract and (for an opposing view) http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/env.1149/full

Third, there is more to these methods (occupancy, Nmix models) than just running a canned function in R. It would be good it you could read up on them to improve your understanding of the basics.
 
Best regards  --  Marc
